title: Numbers to Know and Estimation
summary: Turn daily users into QPS, storage and bandwidth. Use rough latency and capacity numbers to make a decision, not to fill a page with arithmetic.
body:
Use a rough estimate to answer a practical question: what does the simple design need next? If one primary handles 2,000 writes per second, there is no throughput reason to shard yet. If a year of data is 300 TB and exceeds your node's storage budget, a clever schema alone will not make it fit. The interview goal is not perfect arithmetic. It is knowing roughly what common components can handle and using that comparison to make a choice. Here are the reference numbers and a method you can reuse.

## The latency ladder

Memorise orders of magnitude, not exact nanoseconds. Hardware changes; the gaps between rungs are what drive design.

| Operation | Rough latency | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU L1 cache reference | ~1 ns | In-process work is effectively free next to I/O |
| Main memory reference | ~100 ns | An in-memory hash lookup is far cheaper than any network call |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM | ~10–50 µs | Scanning megabytes in memory is fine per request |
| NVMe SSD random read (4 KB) | ~20–100 µs | Index lookups that miss RAM still cost far less than a millisecond |
| Round trip within one datacenter or zone | ~0.2–0.5 ms | Each extra service hop costs about this much, plus processing |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD | ~0.2–1 ms | Large payloads cost more than the hop itself |
| Round trip between zones in one region | ~1–2 ms | Synchronous cross-zone replication is affordable |
| Spinning-disk seek | ~5–10 ms | Random I/O on HDD is why log-structured writes exist |
| Round trip across a continent | ~40–80 ms | Users far from a region feel every extra round trip |
| Round trip between continents | ~100–200 ms | Synchronous cross-region writes add this to every commit |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["RAM lookup ~100 ns"] --> B["SSD read ~100 µs"]
    B --> C["Same-zone RTT ~0.5 ms"]
    C --> D["Cross-zone RTT ~1-2 ms"]
    D --> E["HDD seek ~10 ms"]
    E --> F["Cross-continent RTT ~100+ ms"]
```

Each step to the right is roughly one to three orders of magnitude slower than the one before it. The practical rule: a request that makes five sequential calls inside one zone can still finish in a few milliseconds, but a request that makes five sequential calls across an ocean cannot finish in under half a second. Physics sets the floor: light in fibre travels about 200,000 km/s, so every 1,000 km of path adds roughly 10 ms of round-trip time before any queuing.

## Throughput ballparks per component

These are deliberately conservative single-node figures for simple operations on reasonable hardware. Real numbers depend on payload size, query shape and tuning, so state them as assumptions.

| Component | Comfortable ballpark | Typical reason to go beyond one node |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stateless app server | 1,000–10,000 requests/s | Availability first; CPU-heavy work second |
| Relational DB primary (indexed point ops) | ~5,000–20,000 writes/s, 10,000–50,000 reads/s | Write volume, data size beyond a few TB, or hot rows |
| In-memory cache node (Redis-like) | ~100,000 simple ops/s; tens to a few hundred GB of RAM | Memory size or a single hot key |
| Log/stream broker (Kafka-like) | Hundreds of MB/s per broker; a partition roughly 10 MB/s | Retention size and consumer parallelism |
| Object storage | Effectively unbounded total capacity | Per-prefix request rates and egress cost, not space |
| Network interface | 10 Gbit/s is about 1.25 GB/s | Large media fan-out |

A single well-indexed relational database handles far more than most interview prompts imply. Saying "Postgres tops out at a few hundred writes per second" is a common error that leads to unnecessary sharding.

## Units that save time

- A day has 86,400 seconds; round to 100,000 (10^5). One million events per day is about 12 per second.
- 1 KB × 1 billion = 1 TB. 1 KB × 1 million = 1 GB.
- Bytes versus bits: network links are quoted in bits per second; storage in bytes. Divide bits by 8.
- Powers of two versus ten (KiB versus KB) differ by under 10% at these scales. Ignore the difference and say so.

## From users to queries per second

Start with daily active users (DAU), count their actions and convert the daily total to queries or requests per second (QPS). Add a peak factor, then compare that rate with what one node can handle.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    DAU["Daily active users"] --> ACT["x actions per user per day"]
    ACT --> DAY["Requests per day"]
    DAY --> AVG["/ 86,400 = average QPS"]
    AVG --> PEAK["x peak factor 2-5 = peak QPS"]
    PEAK --> NODES["/ per-node capacity = node count"]
    DAY --> SIZE["x bytes per record = daily storage"]
    SIZE --> TOTAL["x retention x replication = total storage"]
```

The left branch gives throughput and the right branch gives storage. Peak, not average, sizes the fleet: traffic follows time zones and events, so a peak of two to five times the daily average is a reasonable default unless the prompt says otherwise (a ticket on-sale can be 100 times). Replication and retention multiply storage, and indexes typically add another 20–100% on top of raw row size.

Bandwidth follows the same pattern: peak QPS × response size. A feed endpoint returning 50 KB at 20,000 peak QPS sends 1 GB/s, which is about 8 Gbit/s. That number is a strong argument for a CDN or smaller payloads; the request count alone would not have revealed it.

## A worked example

Prompt: a workout-logging app with 20 million daily active users. Each user logs about two workouts per day and opens their history ten times per day. A workout record is roughly 500 bytes. Keep data for five years.

**Writes.** 20M × 2 = 40M writes/day ≈ 40M / 10^5 ≈ 400/s average. With a peak factor of 3, about 1,200 writes/s. *Decision:* one relational primary handles this comfortably. No write sharding is needed for throughput.

**Reads.** 20M × 10 = 200M reads/day ≈ 2,000/s average, about 6,000/s at peak. *Decision:* a single primary could probably serve this, but reads are personal and repetitive, so a cache or one or two read replicas buys headroom and availability. Nothing exotic.

**Storage.** 40M × 500 B = 20 GB/day. × 365 ≈ 7.3 TB/year, ≈ 36 TB over five years before indexes. With three replicas, more than 100 TB of raw disk. *Decision:* this is the number that changes the design. It exceeds what one primary should hold, so either partition by user ID, or keep recent months in the transactional store and move older workouts to cheaper columnar or object storage that history queries can still reach.

**Bandwidth.** A history page of 20 workouts is about 10 KB; 6,000 reads/s × 10 KB = 60 MB/s. *Decision:* none. Mention it and move on.

Notice that only one of four estimates altered the architecture. That is normal, and saying "this one does not change anything" is a perfectly good interview move.

## When to estimate, and when not to

Estimate when the number could change your choice: one node or several, in memory or on disk, synchronous or queued. If every plausible answer leads to the same design, move on. Many interviewers prefer estimates at the moment a choice needs them, rather than a page of totals up front. Say your assumptions aloud, round generously and keep the units next to each number.

## Common errors

| Error | Example | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit slips | Treating a 1 Gbit/s link as 1 GB/s | Write units on every line; divide bits by 8 |
| Average used as peak | Sizing for 400 writes/s when peak is 1,200 | Apply an explicit peak factor and say why |
| Forgotten replication | 36 TB "fits on three 20 TB disks" | Multiply by replica count and add index overhead |
| Ignored fan-out | One post triggers 1,000 feed writes | Multiply by fan-out before comparing with capacity |
| False precision | "11,574 QPS" | Say "about 12,000" and move on |
| Estimate without a decision | Computing storage when nothing depends on it | Tie every number to a choice or drop it |

## How to use it in an interview

Bring up estimation at the moment a choice depends on it: "Before deciding whether to shard, let me check write volume." Show the chain in one line, compare the result with a per-node ballpark, and state the conclusion. Expect follow-ups such as "what if traffic grows 10x?" or "what if a celebrity has 50 million followers?" A good answer reuses the same chain with the new input and identifies which component crosses its threshold first.

## Interview exercise

A photo-sharing service has 50 million daily users. Each uploads 0.2 photos per day (average 2 MB after compression) and views 100 photos per day. Estimate peak upload QPS, daily new storage, and peak egress bandwidth. Which of the three changes your design, and how? Write your arithmetic before checking it against a calculator.

## Further reading

- [Google SRE book: Handling overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/) discusses capacity, load and why per-request cost matters more than request counts.
- [Redis benchmarks documentation](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/benchmarks/) explains how to measure throughput rather than trusting a single figure.
keyTakeaways: Memorise orders of magnitude: RAM ~100 ns, SSD ~100 µs, same-zone round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~100 ms.
A single relational primary handles thousands of writes per second; do not shard before an estimate says so.
Convert users to load with DAU x actions / 86,400 x peak factor, and storage with record size x retention x replication.
Estimate only when the result could fall on either side of a design threshold, and state the decision it drives.
Most estimation mistakes are unit slips, missing peak factors, forgotten replication and ignored fan-out.
